summary:
Nāgāland stands under India's national framework on gender recognition, and no deviation from the national position has been identified for the state at a margin material enough to score separately (within ±0.02). A visitor to Nāgāland therefore faces the same recognition, documentation and policing conditions as elsewhere in India.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Human Rights Watch describes the amendment as a major reversal of the rights affirmed in 2014 and has urged the president not to sign it; the bill had been approved by both houses and was awaiting presidential assent. Mandatory medical certification for identity recognition has been described by critics as an attack on privacy and dignity. The government argues that the narrower definition improves delivery of welfare schemes; critics warn that it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. The Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Facilities and care access are largely set at state level, so the conditions a visitor encounters depend heavily on which state they are in. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras; Nāgāland is not among the states named in the sources as operating such a board.

The national position on recognition is contested terrain. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the March 2026 amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Human Rights Watch's March 2026 intervention places India's 2026 reversal against the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling, which had affirmed self-identification.

Protection machinery also varies by state. The Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma bind police conduct and public authorities in Tamil Nadu, and the same court ordered the Tamil Nadu government in April 2019 to prohibit sex-selective surgery on intersex infants. Reported police treatment of trans people diverges by source: a foreign government's December 2025 policy note finds abuse limited and non-systemic, while documented victim interviews from June 2024 record abusive conduct by railway police towards trans detainees.
localsOnly:
Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and welfare boards in states such as Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha pay pensions, subsidise housing and provide sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals. Several states extend targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits to hijras.

In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries. Court-acknowledged same-sex couples count as family units for some purposes, though no marriage or civil partnership exists.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources contain no Nāgáland-specific material on recognition, identity documents, policing or violence against trans persons; the state position rests entirely on the national framework, and no state-level transgender policy, welfare board or enforcement record for Nāgāland was located in the inventory.

The status of the March 2026 amendment is unresolved in the sources: the bill had passed both houses but presidential assent was still outstanding as of the reporting, so whether and when its recognition and medical-certification provisions take effect is not settled here.

The scale of clandestine conversion-therapy networks operating despite the 2021 and 2022 bans is not sourced, and no figures are available on violence against trans persons in Nāgāland. Whether a short-term visitor can draw on Ayushman Bharat benefits for transition-related care is also not addressed by the sources.
